title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: The sixth day was fixed for the election of the marshal of the province.

The rooms, large and small, were packed with noblemen in every kind of uniform. Many had come just for that day. Men who hadn't seen each other in years — some from the Crimea, some from Petersburg, some from abroad — met in the rooms of the Hall of Nobility. There was a great deal of discussion around the governor's table under the portrait of the Tsar.

The nobles, in both the larger and the smaller rooms, grouped themselves in camps, and from their hostile, suspicious looks, from the silence that fell when outsiders approached a group, and from the way some of them drew off to whisper in the far corridor, it was clear that each side had its own secrets. In appearance the noblemen split sharply into two classes: the old and the new. The old wore for the most part the old-style uniforms of the nobility, buttoned all the way up, with spurs and hats — or else their own naval, cavalry, infantry, or official uniforms. The uniforms of the older men were embroidered in the old fashion, with epaulets on their shoulders; they were unmistakably tight and short in the waist, as if their wearers had outgrown them. The younger men wore the nobility uniform with long waists and broad shoulders, unbuttoned over white waistcoats, or uniforms with black collars and the embroidered insignia of justices of the peace. The court uniforms that brightened up the crowd here and there belonged to the younger set.

But the division between young and old didn't match the division between the parties. Some of the young men, Levin noticed, belonged to the old party; and some of the very oldest noblemen, on the other hand, were whispering with Sviazhsky and were clearly ardent partisans of the new party.

Levin stood in the smaller room, where they were smoking and having light refreshments, close to his own circle, and listening to what they were saying he conscientiously applied his whole mind to working out what was meant. Sergey Ivanovitch was the center around which the others gathered. At that moment he was listening to Sviazhsky and Hliustov, the marshal of another district, who belonged to their party. Hliustov refused to go with his district to ask Snetkov to stand, while Sviazhsky was trying to persuade him to do so, and Sergey Ivanovitch approved the plan. Levin couldn't work out why the opposition would ask the marshal to stand when they wanted to replace him.
Stepan Arkadyevitch, who had just finished a drink and a bite of lunch, came up to them in his uniform of a gentleman of the bedchamber, wiping his lips with a perfumed, hemmed batiste handkerchief.
"We are deploying our forces," he said, tugging at his whiskers. "Sergey Ivanovitch!"
And after listening to the conversation, he came down on Sviazhsky's side.
"One district is enough, and Sviazhsky is obviously in opposition," he said — words evidently clear to everyone but Levin.

"Why, Kostya, you here too! Don't tell me you've been converted, eh?" he added, turning to Levin and slipping his arm through his. Levin would gladly have been converted, but he couldn't make out the point at issue, and stepping a few paces away from the others, he explained to Stepan Arkadyevitch his inability to see why the marshal of the province had to be asked to stand.

_"O sancta simplicitas!"_ said Stepan Arkadyevitch, and briefly, clearly, he explained it. If, as in previous elections, every district asked the marshal of the province to stand, he would be elected without a ballot. That mustn't happen. Now eight districts had agreed to call on him: if two refused, Snetkov might decline to stand at all, and then the old party could pick another of their own, which would throw the whole calculation off. But if only one district — Sviazhsky's — did not call on him, Snetkov would let himself go to a ballot. Some of them were even going to vote for him on purpose, and let him pick up a good many votes, so the enemy would be thrown off the scent, and when a candidate from the other side was put up, they could give him some votes too. Levin understood up to a point, but not entirely, and was about to ask a few more questions when suddenly everyone started talking at once and making a racket, and they moved into the big room.

"What is it? Eh? Who?" "No guarantee? Whose? What?" "They won't pass him?" "No guarantee?" "They won't let Flerov in?" "Because of the charge against him?" "At this rate they won't admit anyone. It's a swindle!" "The law!" Levin heard exclamations from every side, and he moved into the big room with everyone else, all of them hurrying somewhere, afraid of missing something. Squeezed by the crowding noblemen, he made his way to the high table where the marshal of the province, Sviazhsky, and the other leaders were hotly debating something.
